hypothesis.title: Iterative Feedback-Driven Agent Refinement for Multi-Task Generalization
hypothesis.summary: We propose a framework where LLM agents iteratively refine their outputs using self-generated feedback, bypassing traditional supervised fine-tuning. By simulating multi-turn interactions with environment feedback, agents develop task-agnostic refinement capabilities. The approach is validated on AgentBench tasks, comparing performance against static prompting and fine-tuned baselines using success rate and reasoning error metrics.
hypothesis.gap: Existing multi-agent systems (ref-012, ref-021, ref-031) assume fixed workflows and lack mechanisms for agents to autonomously improve through self-feedback.
hypothesis.approach: Implement a self-refinement loop where agents generate intermediate solutions, critique their own outputs, and iteratively improve based on simulated environment feedback (ref-008, ref-035, ref-069). The framework uses a single LLM as both generator and critic without human intervention.
hypothesis.evaluation: Compare against static prompting and fine-tuned baselines on AgentBench tasks. Metrics include success rate, reasoning error rate, and task generalization across unseen domains. Use GPT-4 as the evaluation judge for solution correctness.

The 'simulated environment feedback' is undefined, and the 'task-agnostic refinement capabilities' claim is not tested with a controlled experiment comparing fixed vs. adaptive workflows.

refined.title: Dynamic Workflow Adaptation in Multi-Agent Systems via Self-Refinement
refined.summary: We propose a framework where LLM-based multi-agent systems adapt their workflows through iterative self-refinement, using environment feedback to update task plans. Unlike prior work that relies on static collaboration patterns, our approach enables agents to dynamically adjust their interaction patterns and solution strategies. The method is evaluated on AgentBench tasks, comparing against fixed multi-agent baselines and self-refinement systems using success rate, reasoning error rate, and workflow adaptability metrics.
refined.gap: While ref-012, ref-021, and ref-031 enable multi-agent collaboration, they assume static workflows and lack mechanisms for agents to autonomously update their interaction patterns based on environment feedback. Ref-035 enables self-refinement but does not integrate it with multi-agent collaboration. No prior work combines dynamic workflow adaptation with self-refinement in multi-agent systems.
refined.approach: Implement a three-phase process: 1) Task decomposition using a coordinator agent, 2) Parallel solution generation by specialized agents, 3) Iterative refinement where agents critique and update their own and others' outputs using environment feedback. The coordinator dynamically adjusts agent roles and interaction patterns based on solution quality. The system uses a single LLM (GPT-4) for all agents, with a fixed prompt structure for self-critique and feedback integration.
refined.evaluation: Evaluate on 4 diverse tasks from AgentBench (ref-041): code generation, web navigation, math reasoning, and interactive QA. Compare against: 1) Static multi-agent baselines (ref-012, ref-021), 2) Single-agent self-refinement (ref-035), 3) Fixed workflow self-refinement. Metrics: success rate, reasoning error rate (count of incorrect intermediate steps in successful solutions), and workflow adaptability (number of role/interaction changes). Use GPT-4 as judge for solution correctness, with 3 independent evaluations per solution.

hypothesis.title: Iterative Feedback Refinement for LLM-Based Scientific Visualization Agents
hypothesis.summary: This paper proposes integrating self-refinement mechanisms into LLM-based visualization agents to iteratively improve plot quality through automated feedback loops. The approach combines code generation with runtime error correction and visual feedback analysis to address persistent inaccuracies in scientific data visualization. Evaluation uses MatPlotBench with metrics comparing output fidelity to human-verified ground truth, demonstrating improved accuracy over static generation baselines.
hypothesis.gap: Existing LLM visualization frameworks lack mechanisms for iterative refinement based on execution feedback, leading to persistent errors in complex plots.
hypothesis.approach: Implement a feedback loop where generated code is executed, visual outputs are analyzed for anomalies, and the LLM receives structured feedback to regenerate corrected code. Incorporates both syntactic error checking and semantic validation of visual elements.
hypothesis.evaluation: Compare against MatPlotAgent baselines using MatPlotBench metrics (structural accuracy, data fidelity) and GPT-4V scoring. Measure reduction in error propagation through multiple refinement iterations.

refined.title: Semantic Validation-Driven Iterative Refinement for LLM-Based Scientific Visualization
refined.summary: This paper proposes integrating semantic validation of visual elements into LLM-based visualization agents to iteratively improve plot quality. The approach extends MatPlotAgent's visual feedback mechanism by adding structured semantic checks for data-plot consistency, addressing its limitation in detecting high-level visual-semantic mismatches. Evaluation uses MatPlotBench with metrics comparing output fidelity to human-verified ground truth, demonstrating improved accuracy over MatPlotAgent's native feedback system.
refined.gap: MatPlotAgent (ref-001) detects low-level execution errors but lacks semantic validation of visual elements, failing to identify high-level mismatches between data and plot interpretations (e.g., incorrect axis scaling, misrepresented trends).
refined.approach: Extend MatPlotAgent's feedback loop with a semantic validation module that (1) extracts visual features from generated plots, (2) compares them against expected data characteristics (e.g., trend direction, magnitude ranges), and (3) generates structured feedback for code regeneration. Uses GPT-4V for feature extraction and comparison, with feedback formatted as ["element_type", "expected_value", "actual_value", "severity"] tuples.
refined.evaluation: Compare against MatPlotAgent baselines on MatPlotBench using (1) structural accuracy (axis labels, tick positions), (2) data fidelity (point deviation from ground truth), and (3) semantic correctness (trend/relationship mismatches). Measure improvement across refinement iterations with ablation study isolating semantic validation contribution.

hypothesis.title: Dynamic Agent Pruning for Cost-Effective Multi-Agent Collaboration via Reinforcement Learning
hypothesis.summary: This paper proposes a reinforcement learning framework to dynamically prune redundant agents in multi-agent systems during task execution, reducing computational costs while maintaining performance. The approach uses a learned policy to evaluate agent contributions in real-time, removing those with minimal impact. It will be validated on collaborative coding and scientific visualization tasks from MatPlotBench and ChatDev, comparing agent count reduction, cost savings, and task accuracy against static agent baselines.
hypothesis.gap: Existing multi-agent systems (ref-002, ref-024) use static structures that fail to adapt to task complexity, incurring unnecessary costs. No work measures how dynamic agent removal affects performance-cost tradeoffs in real-world settings.
hypothesis.approach: A reinforcement learning agent trained to predict task-relevant agent contributions, with a pruning mechanism that removes low-impact agents during execution. The policy is optimized using reward signals based on task accuracy and agent count reduction.
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include static agent systems (ref-002) and random pruning. Metrics: (1) task success rate, (2) token cost reduction, (3) agent utilization efficiency. Tested on MatPlotBench visualization tasks and ChatDev software development scenarios.

refined.title: Dynamic Agent Pruning for Cost-Effective Multi-Agent Collaboration via Reinforcement Learning
refined.summary: This paper proposes a reinforcement learning framework to dynamically prune redundant agents in multi-agent systems during task execution, reducing computational costs while maintaining performance. The approach uses a learned policy to evaluate agent contributions in real-time, removing those with minimal impact. It will be validated on collaborative coding and scientific visualization tasks from MatPlotBench and ChatDev, comparing agent count reduction, cost savings, and task accuracy against static agent baselines.
refined.gap: While ref-002 introduces a dynamic orchestrator that adaptively sequences agents, it does not measure how selective agent removal impacts performance-cost tradeoffs. No work evaluates pruning mechanisms that explicitly remove low-contribution agents during execution, leaving open the question of whether targeted removal can further reduce costs without compromising task success.
refined.approach: A reinforcement learning agent trained to predict task-relevant agent contributions, with a pruning mechanism that removes agents whose contribution to task reward falls below a threshold ε for τ consecutive steps. The policy uses a reward function R = α * task_accuracy - β * active_agents, where α and β balance accuracy and cost. The state space includes agent activity logs and partial task outputs; actions select agents to retain or remove.
refined.evaluation: Baselines include ref-002's orchestrator (without pruning) and random pruning. Metrics: (1) task success rate, (2) token cost reduction, (3) agent utilization efficiency (correct actions / total agent actions). Tested on MatPlotBench visualization tasks and ChatDev software development scenarios. Ablation study compares performance with/without pruning while keeping the orchestrator active.

hypothesis.title: Dynamic Agent Pruning for Resource-Constrained Multi-Agent Collaboration

The approach uses a lightweight orchestrator to evaluate agent contributions and remove non-essential participants. Evaluated on ChatDev tasks, it demonstrates comparable performance to full systems at reduced cost.

refined.title: Dynamic Agent Pruning via Cost-Benefit Analysis for Multi-Agent Collaboration
refined.summary: We introduce a method to dynamically prune redundant agents in multi-agent systems during task execution by evaluating their marginal contributions using a lightweight orchestrator. The approach combines task progress metrics with agent-specific performance indicators to identify non-essential agents for removal. Evaluated on ChatDev tasks, it achieves comparable performance to full systems at reduced computational cost.
refined.gap: Existing dynamic multi-agent frameworks (ref-002, ref-042, ref-044) optimize agent coordination but lack explicit mechanisms to remove agents entirely based on their marginal contributions during task execution. Ref-002 prioritizes agents but doesn't eliminate them, ref-042 prunes messages but not agents, and ref-044 explores scaling but doesn't dynamically reduce agent counts.
refined.approach: Implement a lightweight orchestrator that computes a cost-benefit score for each agent at discrete intervals using: (1) task progress metrics (percentage of subtasks completed), (2) agent-specific performance indicators (number of successful contributions vs. errors), and (3) computational cost (tokens consumed). Agents with negative marginal contribution (benefit < cost) are pruned. The orchestrator uses a threshold-based decision rule: if (current benefit / current cost) < (historical average benefit / historical average cost), the agent is removed. This differs from ref-002's prioritization and ref-042's message-level pruning by focusing on agent-level removal based on quantified marginal utility.
refined.evaluation: Measure task success rate, computational cost (tokens used), and convergence speed (number of iterations to completion) on ChatDev software development tasks (ref-031). Compare against: (1) static multi-agent baseline (ref-031's full agent configuration), (2) ref-042's AgentPrune (message-level pruning), and (3) human-designed minimal configurations (5 experts selecting optimal agent subsets). Ablation study isolates pruning mechanism by comparing dynamic vs. static agent counts with identical agent implementations.

hypothesis.title: Causal Misidentification Mitigation in Multi-Agent Collaborative Systems
hypothesis.summary: This work addresses spurious correlations in multi-agent collaborative frameworks by introducing causal structure identification modules that prevent error propagation during task decomposition. The method uses environment interaction data to distinguish causal from coincidental feature correlations, improving task success in complex workflows.
hypothesis.gap: Current multi-agent systems fail to account for causal relationships between agent actions and environmental states, leading to suboptimal coordination in long-horizon tasks.
hypothesis.approach: Augment agent communication protocols with causal inference components that track action-outcome dependencies. Agents perform targeted interventions to validate hypothesized causal relationships before committing to multi-step plans.
hypothesis.evaluation: Benchmark on ChatDev software development tasks with metrics tracking task success rate, plan revision frequency, and error propagation distance. Compare against MetaGPT and ChatDev baselines.

assumption.unsupported: The hypothesis claims 'Current multi-agent systems fail to account for causal relationships between agent actions and environmental states, leading to suboptimal coordination in long-horizon tasks.' hypothesis.title: Process-Supervised Reinforcement Learning for Mathematical Reasoning

Unlike outcome-based methods, the approach provides step-level feedback through a learned reward model trained on synthetic process annotations. Experiments on GSM8K and MATH show 10.4% and 4.4% accuracy improvements over outcome-supervised baselines, with further gains from verification-based reranking.

hypothesis.approach: A synthetic process annotation generator creates step-level labels for training a reward model, which then provides feedback for proximal policy optimization (PPO) fine-tuning of LLMs.
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include outcome-supervised PPO and chain-of-thought prompting. Metrics are accuracy on GSM8K and MATH datasets, with ablation studies on reward model quality.

hypothesis.title: Adaptive Agent Orchestration for Long-Tail Knowledge Retrieval
hypothesis.summary: This work introduces an adaptive agent orchestration framework that dynamically routes queries to specialized knowledge agents based on confidence scores and long-tail knowledge frequency. The system combines retrieval-augmented generation with reinforcement learning to optimize agent selection for rare knowledge domains.
hypothesis.gap: Current LLM-based agents fail to effectively retrieve and synthesize long-tail knowledge due to static agent hierarchies and lack of dynamic resource allocation.
hypothesis.approach: A puppeteer-style orchestrator assigns queries to agents based on (1) pre-training data frequency estimates and (2) real-time confidence calibration. Agents specialize in knowledge domains with varying frequency distributions, and the orchestrator learns to route queries through reinforcement learning with a reward function based on retrieval accuracy and response novelty.
hypothesis.evaluation: Baselines include static agent chains and single-agent retrieval systems. Metrics are TriviaQA accuracy for rare entities, BLEU-4 for response diversity, and latency per query. Synthetic long-tail datasets test scalability.

refined.title: Dynamic Agent Routing for Long-Tail Knowledge Retrieval
refined.summary: This work introduces a dynamic agent routing framework that directs queries to specialized knowledge agents based on pre-training data frequency estimates and real-time confidence calibration. hypothesis.title: Reward Model Bootstrapping for Long-Tail Knowledge Acquisition
hypothesis.summary: This paper proposes using outcome-supervised value models (OVM) to address long-tail knowledge gaps in LLMs. The hypothesis is that training reward models on final answer correctness enables effective process supervision without step-level annotations. The approach combines outcome-based reinforcement learning with iterative feedback to reinforce correct reasoning paths. Experiments on GSM8K and MATH demonstrate improved performance on low-frequency problem types compared to outcome-only or process-supervised baselines.

hypothesis.evaluation: Compare against outcome-only RL, process-supervised RL, and standard fine-tuning on GSM8K/MATH. Metrics: accuracy on low-frequency problem clusters, reward model calibration, and generalization to unseen problem types. Use SciBench as out-of-distribution test set.
